analysis.one_liner: Strips the labor board of its power to prosecute employers for unfair labor practices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so the National Labor Relations Board could investigate unfair labor practices but could not stop them or punish them. It removes the Board's General Counsel's power to file and prosecute complaints, bars the Board from issuing any rules that affect workers' or employers' rights, and instead lets individuals sue employers in federal district court. Under current law, a worker who is fired for organizing a union can file a free charge and the Board prosecutes it; this bill would replace that with private lawsuits the worker must bring and pay for.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers accused of unfair labor practices, such as firing workers for union activity or refusing to bargain. They would no longer face a federal agency that investigates, prosecutes, and can order them to stop violations, and the Board could no longer write rules like its election-procedure rules.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the General Counsel's authority to issue and prosecute unfair labor practice complaints before the Board, so no federal prosecutor would pursue these cases. [S2]
Removes the Board's power to prevent any person from engaging in an unfair labor practice, leaving it with power only to investigate. [S2][S3]

Limits Board rulemaking to its internal functions and forbids any rules affecting the substantive or procedural rights of employers, employees, or unions, including rules on elections and unfair labor practices. [S2][S3]
Replaces Board enforcement with private civil actions in federal district court, where an aggrieved person could seek relief including an injunction. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Workers and unions, who would lose free, expedited enforcement of their organizing and bargaining rights and would have to file and finance their own federal lawsuits instead.

drawbacks.text: Private lawsuits are slower, more expensive, and harder to bring than the current system, in which a worker files a charge and the Board's General Counsel investigates and prosecutes at no cost; low-wage workers rarely have the resources to litigate in district court. [S2]

Without the Board's power to prevent violations or issue rules, there would be no agency mechanism to quickly stop ongoing violations such as unlawful firings during a union drive, and no unified rules for representation elections. [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit flows to employers, who would gain near-total immunity from federal labor-law prosecution, and to opponents of Board rulemaking. The cost falls on workers, whose organizing and bargaining rights would become largely unenforceable except through individual lawsuits most cannot afford to bring.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on September 28, 2015, with original cosponsors including Sens. Ted Cruz and Tom Cotton. [S3]
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. [S5]
Three Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill. [S4]
No Democratic senator cosponsored the bill. [S4]
The committee took no further action; the bill had no vote in either chamber and expired at the end of the 114th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions kept the existing labor board enforcement system, and employers did not gain the bill's protections. The three Republican sponsors gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, since the enforcement system stayed intact

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the bill died in committee with no votes in either chamber.

industries.industry: Employers with unionized or organizing workforces
industries.note: The bill would eliminate federal prosecution and prevention of unfair labor practices and block Board rulemaking, leaving workers to enforce their own rights through costly private lawsuits. The industry's gain comes directly from weaker enforcement of protections for ordinary workers.

Unions rely on the National Labor Relations Board to police employer interference in organizing and bargaining; removing the Board's complaint and enforcement powers would make those rights largely unenforceable.
